021.subtitle: The body totalled up, and the consort finally named

commentary.meaning: Three summarising names, then three that change the subject. The verse opens by totalling the portrait just completed: she is red throughout, there is no limb of hers that could be faulted, and there is no ornament she is not wearing. Two of the three begin with sarva, all, and that is the point — the description has been proceeding part by part for many verses, and it closes by refusing to leave anything out. Then the frame widens. Having been described alone, she is suddenly not alone: she is on the lap of Śiva in his form as the lord of desire. The name that follows is two syllables long, the shortest thing in this stretch of the hymn, and it simply gives her his name in the feminine. The last name reverses the arrangement once more — he may be her seat, but he is hers, held by nothing except his own attachment. This is the fifty-fourth name and the last one that concerns her person. The verse after it leaves her body altogether and begins on the mountain where she lives.
commentary.history:
Aruṇa is the red of the sky immediately before sunrise, distinguished in Sanskrit from rakta and lohita, which are simply red, and from the words for crimson and scarlet. It is also a proper name: Aruṇa is the dawn personified, the charioteer of the sun, hatched prematurely from Vinatā's egg and so incomplete in body, elder brother of Garuḍa. The colour saturates Śrīvidyā's iconography. Her body is red, her garment is red, the unguent smeared on her is red, the flowers offered to her are red, the throne is red; the meditation verses prefixed to this very hymn open by calling her aruṇā before saying anything else. The usual explanation refers the colour to rajas, the guṇa of activity and passion, since she is the aspect of the absolute that acts rather than the one that rests; commentators frequently hear karuṇā, compassion, behind aruṇā as well. The name insists on uniformity: not red ornaments on a fair body, but red without interruption, which is a way of saying that nothing about her is neutral or inert.

Anavadyāṅgī rewards being taken apart. Avadya is a gerundive of the root vad, to speak, with a negative prefix — literally "not to be spoken of," hence disgraceful, the sort of thing one does not mention. Anavadya negates that again, so the word means blameless by a double negative, with a faint sense of "there is nothing here one would need to be tactful about." It is an old word, at home in Vedic, and a stock epithet in court poetry. Its work here is structural: after all the individual limbs have been described, one name certifies the whole. Sarvābharaṇabhūṣitā continues that certification into the jewellery. Ābharaṇa comes from a root meaning to carry or bring, so an ornament is literally something brought and put on, and the offering of ābharaṇa is one of the standard services in the sixteenfold liturgy — the name describes something the worshipper does rather than only something to picture. Commentators regularly turn it around: it is not that the ornaments adorn her, but that anything she wears becomes an ornament.

With the fourth name the hymn introduces her consort under the title Śrīvidyā always uses for him. Kāmeśvara means lord of desire, and the title carries a story. When the gods needed Śiva roused from his meditation so that a son could be born to destroy the demon Tāraka, they sent Kāma, the god of desire, to shoot him; Śiva opened his third eye and burnt Kāma to ash on the spot, and at the pleading of Kāma's wife Rati restored him without a body, whence his name Ananga, the limbless one. In this tradition Śiva does not merely defeat desire and leave it destroyed; he becomes its sovereign, and Lalitā is Kāmeśvarī, the feminine of the same word. The two occupy the bindu, the central point of the Śrīcakra, and the school's position on pleasure follows from that arrangement: desire is not to be extinguished but ruled, and rule of it is what divinity looks like. Aṅka, the word for lap, means the hollow of the side where a child is carried, and the iconography is literal — she sits on his left thigh. The couch on which the two of them sit will be described much later in the hymn, when its four legs turn out to be four of the great gods.

Śivā is the feminine of śiva, and the history of that adjective is worth knowing. Śiva means auspicious, kindly, benign, and in the Vedic hymns it is applied to the fierce god Rudra as a propitiating euphemism long before it hardens into his proper name; the word never entirely sheds that ambiguity. To give the goddess the bare feminine of the god's name is the strongest identity claim in the verse, and the tradition presses it. The commonplace in tantric literature is that śiva without śakti is śava, a corpse — a pun that turns on a single vowel and that the Saundaryalaharī opens by asserting in more decorous language.

Svādhīnavallabhā, the last of the six, is a technical term borrowed from poetics. The handbooks of literary theory classify heroines into eight types according to their situation with respect to the beloved, and the first and happiest is the svādhīnabhartṛkā, the woman whose husband is entirely under her sway and has no wish to be elsewhere. Applying the category to the goddess does two things at once. On the surface it completes the domestic picture. Beneath it, it states the doctrine the whole system rests on, that the inert absolute has no capacity to act except through its own power, so that dependence runs from him to her and not the reverse.
commentary.practice:
The first line contains a piece of orthography that puzzles nearly every beginner. Sarvāruṇā ends in long ā and anavadyāṅgī begins in short a; when a long ā meets a short a, the short vowel disappears entirely, and Devanāgarī records its disappearance with the mark ऽ, the avagraha. It is not a letter and it is not pronounced. What you say is sarvāruṇānavadyāṅgī, one continuous stream, and what the mark tells you is that a vowel was there and has gone. This matters for the nāmāvalī, where the two names come apart again and are recited separately as sarvāruṇāyai namaḥ and anavadyāṅgyai namaḥ.

That second dative is the trap of the verse. Every other name here is a feminine ā-stem taking -āyai, but anavadyāṅgī is an ī-stem, and ī-stems form the dative in -yai: anavadyāṅgyai, not the anavadyāṅgyāyai that reciters reaching for the familiar ending tend to produce.

The verse gives good practice on the guttural nasal ṅ, which occurs twice and in both possible environments — before g in anavadyāṅgī and before k in śivakāmeśvarāṅkasthā. It is the sound at the end of English "sing"; the difficulty is only that Sanskrit puts it inside words where English speakers substitute n. Say aṅgī and aṅka with the tongue tip nowhere near the teeth.

All three Sanskrit sibilants appear here and should be kept apart. Dental s opens sarva and svādhīna, and is the ordinary English s with the tongue at the teeth; palatal ś opens śiva and the śva of kāmeśvara, close to English sh but with the tongue flat against the hard palate; retroflex ṣ appears in bhūṣitā, made with the tongue tip curled back. Running sarvābharaṇabhūṣitā slowly is a compact drill for the first and the third.

Two clusters need care. Sthā in āṅkasthā is dental s followed by aspirated dental th — one puff of breath after the t, not a separate h. Svā at the head of svādhīnavallabhā is s followed by v, both fully articulated, with no vowel slipped between them. Vallabhā has a doubled l, and the doubling is real: hold the l noticeably longer than a single one, as in the join of English "tall lady".

The second line is rhythmically unlike anything nearby: three names of nine, two and six syllables, with the two-syllable śivā between the long ones and easy to swallow. Give it its own space. It is the hymn's shortest utterance set two verses from its longest, and hearing that contrast is part of hearing the verse.

As for what the verse asks: it is the place where the practitioner stops looking at her and notices that someone else has been in the frame the whole time. Everything before this has been a solitary figure being described from the hair downward. From here the object of contemplation is a pair, and the relation between the two is the subject of most of what the hymn goes on to say. Readers who are counting will also notice that this is the fifty-fourth name — half of one hundred and eight, and the point at which the description of her person is finished and the description of her world begins.

crossReferences.deva: शिवः शक्त्या युक्तो यदि भवति शक्तः प्रभवितुं न चेदेवं देवो न खलु कुशलः स्पन्दितुमपि । अतस्त्वामाराध्यां हरिहरविरिञ्चादिभिरपि प्रणन्तुं स्तोतुं वा कथमकृतपुण्यः प्रभवति ॥
crossReferences.iast: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api | atas tvām ārādhyāṃ hariharaviriñcādibhir api praṇantuṃ stotuṃ vā katham akṛtapuṇyaḥ prabhavati ||
crossReferences.translation: Only when he is joined to his power is Śiva able to act; without that, the god cannot so much as stir. You, then, are the one to be worshipped even by Hari and Hara and the creator. How should a man who has done nothing to deserve it manage to bow to you, or to praise you?
crossReferences.relevance: The doctrinal content of svādhīnavallabhā, argued rather than pictured. The poem's opening verse establishes the dependence in the direction the sahasranāma's name assumes, and it also supplies the background for śivā: if he cannot move without her, then his name in the feminine is not a courtesy title. Note that the argument is put in terms of capacity, śakti and śakta from the same root, which is untranslatable but audible in the Sanskrit.

crossReferences.deva: सर्वमङ्गलमाङ्गल्ये शिवे सर्वार्थसाधिके । शरण्ये त्र्यम्बके गौरि नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते ॥
crossReferences.iast: sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye śive sarvārthasādhike | śaraṇye tryambake gauri nārāyaṇi namo'stu te ||
crossReferences.translation: You in whom every good thing finds its own goodness, auspicious one, accomplisher of every purpose, refuge, three-eyed one, pale one — Nārāyaṇī, homage to you.
crossReferences.relevance: Probably the single most widely recited verse addressed to the goddess in India, and it uses śive as a vocative in exactly the sense the fifty-third name uses śivā. It is worth setting beside this verse because it shows that the name is not the property of one school: the Devī Māhātmya, several centuries older and belonging to a different current of goddess worship, already treats the feminine of Śiva's name as a natural address.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The clearest English account of who Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī are and why this tradition places a couple, rather than a single figure, at the centre of its diagram. Brooks is also good on the awkward question of how a school that is doctrinally about desire relates to the ascetic strands of Śaivism around it.

references.title: Śiva: The Erotic Ascetic
references.author: Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty (Oxford University Press, 1973; originally Asceticism and Eroticism in the Mythology of Śiva)
references.note: The book to read on the burning of Kāma and on the contradiction that the title Kāmeśvara resolves. Doniger tracks the story through its many Purāṇic versions and shows that the tension between the god who incinerates desire and the god who is its lord is not a later embarrassment but the engine of the mythology from the start.

references.title: Sāhityadarpaṇa of Viśvanātha
references.author: Viśvanātha Kavirāja (14th c.), available in several editions with English translation
references.note: Where the eightfold classification of heroines is set out, including the svādhīnabhartṛkā whose name the hymn borrows for svādhīnavallabhā. Reading the eight types in order takes ten minutes and permanently changes how the devotional poetry sounds, because you can then hear which literary situation a given verse is placing the goddess in.

references.title: Encountering the Goddess: A Translation of the Devī-Māhātmya and a Study of Its Interpretation
references.author: Thomas B. Coburn (SUNY Press, 1991)
references.note: A reliable translation of the Devī Māhātmya with a long study attached. The chapters on how the text was received and ritualised are the useful part here, since they explain how a verse like the Nārāyaṇī Stuti quoted above came to be recited by people who would not describe themselves as Śāktas at all.

references.title: The Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Vaman Shivaram Apte
references.note: Better than Monier-Williams for this verse because Apte quotes literary usage. The entries for aruṇa, vallabha and śiva show the words at work in poetry rather than only in glossaries, which is where the difference between aruṇa and the other red words becomes visible.
